item.title: REVIEW: HoverAir Versa review: Convenience and creativity with compromises
item.description:
Source: Engadget
HoverAir Versa review: Convenience and creativity with compromises The device is a clever combination that makes a lot of sense, but don’t expect the best of both worlds. Calling a drone a "flying camera" is a bit like calling a small plane a "flying car." If your only option is to fly it, it's just a drone. But what if it was an actual camera, that could also fly? Enter the HoverAir Versa ($539), which is exactly that. The Versa is a handheld gimbal camera similar to DJI's Pocket 4 or the Insta360 Luna Pro. Snap on a magnetic accessory, though, and it becomes a mini drone or... a flying camera. HoverAir isn't new to the game, with its debut Passport selfie drone launching over 10 years ago. The Versa is the company's first stab at a handheld camera though, and there's already a small speed bump. Due to an FCC take-backsie, the Versa's US availability is unclear. The handheld camera could be available at some point, but the drone feature is causing the same legal tangles that cleared shelves of DJI products in the US. Most of the rest of the world, including Canada (and thus eBay resellers no doubt), will have access to the full kit. The 2-in1 is an intuitive idea, but it does raise some questions. Are there compromises in either mode? Can a company far smaller than DJI beat them at their own game? A couple of weeks with the Versa revealed a surprising answer. What exactly is the HoverAir Versa? First and foremost, the Versa is a camera. It has a max resolution of 4K/60 fps combined with a 1/1.3-inch sensor. That puts it somewhere between the Pocket 4 (1-inch) and the Neo 2 (½-inch) in terms of pixel size and low-light performance. The camera has 2x (in-sensor) zoom, will support H-Log in a future update and includes a 10-bit HDR mode. The gimbal is 3-axis, the same as its handheld rivals from DJI and Insta360, but one more axis than the Neo 2 — which is DJI's most comparable drone right now. HoverAir claims the Versa has 17.5 stops of dynamic range, which was one of the main selling points of DJI's pricier Osmo Pocket 4P, though photos are limited to 12 megapixels. There's 55GB of available internal storage, expandable by SD card. Of course, the Versa is more than just a gimbal camera, and its ability to pull double duty comes with a notable perk. In drone mode, the Versa has swappable batteries. That's essential for a drone, but pretty rare for a handheld gimbal camera. Pop the propellers on and, instead of the usual preview on the 1.64-inch screen, you'll see a menu to switch between a set of preset flight patterns. The drone has downward sensors for maintaining position and palm takeoff/landing, but there's zero obstacle avoidance. In follow mode, it uses software smarts to track your path from behind. If it's in front of you, though, things are a little more dicey as it'll track you via the camera but has no idea what's behind it. The Versa's design in handheld mode is pretty boxy. I'm going to assume this comes down to aerodynamics, as it's not particularly stylish. The 1.64-inch display is practical but noticeably cramped if you're used to either the Osmo Pocket 4 or the Luna Pro's larger 2-inch screens. HoverAir states that the Versa has a 19mm equivalent lens with an f2.0 aperture. That's similar to the Luna Pro (f1.8/20mm) and Osmo Pocket 4 (f2.0/20mm), but that 1mm makes all the difference as the Versa shoots noticeably wider. There's also an ultra-wide mode for a more "action-cam" style point of view. The 2x zoom is functional and adds some flexibility to your shot options, but there's no smooth zoom in or out. It's 1x zoom or 2x and nothing in between. The footage from the Versa is sharp and the gimbal smooths things out in a natural way, but the color balance feels a little less natural than its DJI and Insta360s rivals. Outdoors, in bright sunlight, the blue of the sky is heavily saturated. Indoors, I found the image a little warm, with white walls taking a slightly beige hue. The 4K videos look clear and detailed, but with everything in focus, they feel more like something from a high-end action camera rather than a current-gen pocket camera, the latter tends to include a small amount of subject separation. Attaching the flight kit is incredibly simple and drives home the key selling point of the Versa: It's genuinely two products in one. In drone mode, the Versa looks a lot like HoverAir's X1 and X1 Pro Max, complete with the durable, but flexible, prop cage. There may not be obstacle avoidance, but if the Versa does take a ding it shouldn't cause, or take, any damage. As with most drones this size, the Versa is designed to be flown without a controller. You primarily fly through one of the preset modes: hover in place, follow, orbit and so on. There is the option for manual flight via the app and there are controller accessories if you want something a little more tactile. But with the preset modes and gesture control, it's easy to get most tracking or establishing-style shots, which is likely the primary use case for something this size. In the social media age, there is, of course, a vertical shooting mode and there are even some cinematic shots like Dolly zoom and an AI framing mode. Perhaps most curious is the "3D worlds" option that sets the drone to fly around you, and it'll then create a VR-style three-dimensional model that you can export. Just to make sure you know it's not just for realtors, you can add and edit 3D emojis before export. It's fun, and works surprisingly well. I'm not sure I need the emojis though. This is where things get interesting as we have two different categories of rivals to compare it to. At $539, the Versa is taking the $600 Luna Pro almost head on. And it's a tough fight, as the Luna Pro shoots up to 8K video (plus 50-megapixel photos), has a larger 1-inch sensor, superior slow-mo modes (up to 120 fps) and a slew of other video modes and features. DJI's Pocket 4 also out-specs the Versa almost across the board, though price will vary depending on where you're sourcing one in the US Here is where things are a little more complicated as to buy this as a drone, you need to buy the camera plus the flight kit (or a bundle where available). The cheapest bundle costs $649. The Neo 2, despite no official US availability, can be found on Amazon for $300. HoverAir's own X1 Promax — which has the same 1/1.3 sensor and shoots in 8K — costs $699. The regular X1 Pro, which bests the Versa in some specs like max fps and flight time, but has a smaller sensor and only 32GB of storage, currently costs $499. What the Versa does that its competition doesn't goes beyond the obvious. Yes, it faces arguably superior competition in both modes — even from its sister products. But the Versa shows a smarter way of doing things. A lot of people love the Neo 2, for example, for its portability, and they are happy to take some functional tradeoffs for that convenience. The Versa amplifies that by reducing what you need to carry even further. It's also worth mentioning that, despite lacking a few features in both drone and handheld modes, the Versa has some comprehensive accessories at launch. For starters, there's an official ND filter kit, which goes a long way to elevating the camera's cinematic potential. HoverAir also sent over a magnetic tripod accessory that includes a tripod thread which further expands its usefulness. Plus there's a tiny handheld controller that enhances the drone experience enough that it doesn't just feel like an add-on. The Versa supports external/USB microphones which is pretty vital for a pocket camera these days, but that extends to drone mode, too. HoverAir included noise-cancellation that does an impressive job of eliminating propeller noise, further boosting the Versa's all-in-one vlogging credentials. One small bugbear is that SD cards under 64GB are not supported. It's not a huge deal but, if like me, you have a bunch of 32GB cards in your rotation, it's a minor frustration. If you just want a mini drone or a pocket camera, the Versa doesn't make a strong economic case for itself versus something like the Neo 2. If you were considering buying something like a Pocket 4/Luna Pro and a small drone, then suddenly the economics and the compromises look a little more favorable. What you will get though is a capable gimbal camera that is just at home in your hand as it is following you on the trail. That level of convenience will be compelling to a specific subset of creators and gadget-dads on vacation (like me). If you are in the market for a gimbal camera, the "flying" upgrade is a genuine selling point, but know that there are some real tradeoffs.

item.title: REVIEW: Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI Review: Slim OLED gaming that doesn't last long
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware
The Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI mostly succeeds as a thin-and-light gaming laptop, offering solid RTX 5070 Ti performance, a beautiful 240 Hz OLED display, comfortable input devices, and plentiful ports. Its biggest weakness is ironically its battery life, which falls short of what you'd expect from a system focused on portability. Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test. Not everyone wants a hulking gaming laptop. Some prefer something stealthier. Acer’s Predator Helios Neo 16S AI aims for portability but still packs a Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus processor and Nvidia RTX 5070 Ti graphics into a sub-five-pound package. It also includes plenty of ports and a beautiful 240 Hz OLED display. That hardware gives it plenty to work with, but the question remains whether the Helios Neo 16S AI can still deliver solid gaming performance while being portable. Design of the Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI Acer’s obsidian black chassis maintains the look of the Predator series – angular, dark, and visible in the dark with its illuminated lid logo. At 14.05 x 10.85 x 0.74 inches and 4.85 pounds, it’s respectably trim for a gaming laptop, though the Gigabyte Aero X16 (14 x 9.9 x 0.78 inches, 4.2 pounds) and the HyperX Omen 15 (13.5 x 9.96 x 0.93 inches, 4.89 pounds) both have about an inch less depth since neither use a rear thermal shelf like Acer. The build quality is decent – both the chassis and lid show little flex. The stamped aluminum panels on the lid bottom and chassis lid aren’t ultra-premium but still beat plastic. One downside is that the metal shows fingerprints easily, which are difficult to clean off. Acer provides an impressive port variety across three sides: Thunderbolt 4, three USB-A 3.2, USB-C 3.2, HDMI 2.1, 2.5 Gbps Ethernet, a MicroSD card reader, and an audio jack. The rear ports conveniently leave cables out of sight. Inside, the laptop offers Wi-Fi 6E, which isn’t as modern as it could be, though the Killer AX1675i card and accompanying Killer Ethernet jack offer simultaneous network connections via Killer Doubleshot Pro for gamers that want to ensure network priority for the games over one connection and all other apps over the other. It’s also notable that Acer includes a zippered, padded travel sleeve. Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI Specifications Gaming and Graphics on the Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI We tested the Predator Helios Neo 16S AI with a Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus processor, Nvidia RTX 5070 Ti graphics card, and 16GB of RAM. Playing 007 First Light, I saw about 65 to 75 frames per second (FPS) in most scenes, with spikes to over 100 FPS in wide open areas. The game remained all-around playable, though it did require using DLSS to achieve these framerates at native 2560 x 1600 with High settings. Our comparison systems for this Acer are Gigabyte’s Aero X16 (Ryzen AI 7 350, RTX 5070 85W, $1,899.99 when tested, $1,499.99 as of this writing) and HyperX’s Omen 15 (Core Ultra 9 386H, RTX 5070 85W, $2,099.99 when tested, about $3,159.99 as of this writing). Comparisons will focus on the 1920 x 1080 results, but we also included numbers at each laptop’s native resolution: 2560 x 1600 for the Acer and Gigabyte while the HP uses 2880 x 1800. Overall, the Predator Helios Neo 16S AI performed significantly better than both the Gigabyte and HyperX laptops. Much of that has to do with its higher-wattage RTX 5070 Ti, though its Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus processor is also more modern. In Shadow of the Tomb Raider (Highest detail preset), Acer’s 125 FPS at 1080p was on par with the HyperX (126 FPS), though it dominated at its 1600p native resolution, with 76 FPS against Gigabyte’s 60 FPS and HyperX’s 64 FPS. Acer’s advantage continued in Far Cry 6 (Ultra), where it produced 122 FPS to Gigabyte’s 85 FPS and HyperX’s 107 FPS at native resolution. The lead narrowed in Red Dead Redemption 2 (Medium) where Acer and Gigabyte practically tied at 1080p and were within a few FPS at native (52 FPS for Acer and 49 FPS for Gigabyte). The HyperX remained behind. The Acer also demonstrated markedly better performance in Cyberpunk 2077 (Ray Tracing Ultra) particularly at native resolution, where its 21 FPS outran Gigabyte (17 FPS) and HyperX (5 FPS). In Forza Horizon 6 (Extreme), Acer’s 72 FPS at 1080p was strangely lower than HyperX’s 80 FPS, but the results flipped at native, where Acer’s 60 FPS was considerably ahead of HyperX’s 51 FPS. While not a powerhouse, the Predator Helios Neo 16S AI demonstrates competent gaming performance at its 2560 x 1600 native resolution. Crucially, the extra depth from Acer’s thermal shelf design lets its GPU draw 115 W, considerably more than its Gigabyte and HyperX competitors We test the sustained performance of gaming laptops running 15 loops of the Metro: Exodus stress test, simulating half an hour of gaming. During the test, the Predator Helios Neo 16S AI averaged 86.82 FPS across all runs. The variance was less than one FPS between runs, indicating stable thermal performance. The Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus ran at an average of 2.94 GHz on its P-cores, 2.16 GHz on its E-cores, and had an average temperature of 73 degrees Celsius. Meanwhile, the RTX 5070 Ti averaged 1.622 GHz and 74 C. Productivity Performance on the Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI Our Predator Helios Neo 16S AI features a Core Ultra 9 290HX processor, 16GB of dual-channel DDR5-6400 memory, and a 1TB PCIe 4.0 SSD. The Acer’s Core Ultra 9 290HX produced strong numbers in Geekbench. Its single-core score of 3,349 and multi-core score of 19,313 were well ahead of the Ryzen AI 7 350-powered Gigabyte (2,916 and 14,074) and Core Ultra 9 386H-powered HyperX (2,857 and 15,916). This continued into our 4K-to-1080p Handbrake transcoding testing, which Acer dominated with 2 minutes and 30 seconds. The Gigabyte (3:54) and HyperX (3:39) weren’t even close. Acer also produced solid numbers in our 25GB file transfer test, averaging 2,034.84 MBps next to Gigabyte’s1,480.57 MBps and HyperX’s far slower 999.57 MBps. Overall, this Acer is very capable for almost any kind of use. Multitasking will be limited by 16GB of RAM, but Acer sells versions of this laptop with 32GB and it can be upgraded after purchase. Display on the Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI Once glance at this Acer’s display leaves no doubt it’s a key selling point. Its OLED panel technology creates exceptionally vivid colors matched by excellent brightness, and its glossy surface gives it an almost liquid appearance. The 2560 x 1600 resolution is a good balance between detail and what the system’s RTX 5070 Ti graphics card can drive in today’s games. Gamers will also appreciate the smooth 240 Hz refresh rate and Nvidia G-Sync support. (As we’ll see in the battery life section, the screen only supports 240 Hz, resulting in higher-than-expected power consumption.) Watching nature documentaries on National Geographic, I noted the vibrant colors of tropical scenes and the pitch blacks of the depths of the sea. Gaming was equally immersive – 007 First Light felt supremely fluid and looked sharp. I could even make out the writing on character’s uniform badges without zooming. The Acer’s display covered a healthy 82.7% of the DCI-P3 color gamut, matching the Gigabyte, although it wasn’t quite in the same league as the HyperX, which also used an OLED panel. It also didn’t match the HyperX in brightness, but with a peak of 372.4 nits in SDR, the Acer boasts solid brightness for OLED. Our 40% HDR testing revealed up to an impressive 608 nits of brightness. Acer’s keyboard offers a satisfying feel, with ample throw and cushioning without feeling rubbery. In MonkeyType, I reached 116 words per minute with 99% accuracy on my first try, a great result for me on any laptop. The Acer Key app lets you customize the user-customizable key above the plus key, which is handy for creating one-press access to a favorite app or site. Though the keyboard doesn't feature per-key backlighting, its four RGB zones can be set to many patterns and colors in the PredatorSense app. When changing lighting settings, the app initially says they’re controlled by Windows Dynamic Lighting, but that isn’t the case since Dynamic Lighting says no compatible devices are detected. But once dismissing the warning in PredatorSense, the app provides intuitive if limited control over the zones and lid logo. Each zone can be assigned a static lighting effect or the entire keyboard set in a dynamic pattern: breathing, neon, wave, ripple, combo, snake, and disco, with customizable speed, direction, and brightness. Settings can be stored in profiles. Acer also did well with the large touchpad, which offers predictable clicking and my fingers glided smoothly over the matte surface. Audio on the Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI Audio performance isn’t a strong point for the Neo 16S AI. Twin speakers embedded in the palm rest barely have enough volume for casual listening, with average clarity and thin bass. In Phil Collins’ “Don’t Lose My Number”, drum hits sounded flat and vocals were somewhat muted. The speakers are better-suited gaming, offering a decent sense of direction because of their placement on either side of the palm rest, but lack of bass and volume means you'll want a headset. The DTS:X app offers equalizers – without them, the sound is quite tinny. I had the best results leaving the equalizer on Auto. Upgradeability of the Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI With ten Torx T6 screws securing the bottom cover, Acer doesn’t make it easy to get inside the Predator Helios Neo 16S AI. Removing the screws is the easy part – finding an entry point for my plastic pry tool provided harder. I eventually found one at the front corners of the chassis by using mild force. The fact that the side vents are part of the bottom cover compounds the difficulty – I needed to find an opening for my pry tool above those as well. The clips made cringeworthy snapping sounds as they were released, though surprisingly, none cracked off. The effort is not for naught – Acer offers solid upgradeability, with two SODIMM slots under the black plastic cover in the middle, plus an M.2 2280 SSD slot and M.2 2230 wireless card slot. The battery is also replaceable. Battery Life on the Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI Our battery testing consists of web browsing, running OpenGL tests, and streaming videos with the screen at 150 nits while connected to Wi-Fi. The Predator underwhelmed here despite having a large 92 WHr battery – the HyperX laptop outlasted it by almost two hours and the Gigabyte nearly two and a half hours. Most of the blame goes to Acer’s decision to use a screen locked at 240 Hz; more advanced displays would support a variable refresh rate or at least allow it to be lowered to 60 Hz. Heat on the Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI We measure laptop surface temperatures during 15 loops of the Metro: Exodus stress test. During the test, the Acer’s temperatures peaked at 103 degrees F between the keyboard G and H keys, 81 F on the touchpad, and a toasty 129 F on bottom-center. Fan noise is audible particularly while gaming; hearing softer sounds in games will require using a headset. For daily use, the laptop hardly makes any noise. Webcam on the Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI Acer’s 1080p webcam offers a decently sharp picture – I could make out details in my facial hair and eyes from a few feet away. Highlights are also handled reasonably well. It lacks a physical privacy shutter or e-shutter, but it does have infrared (IR) for facial recognition. Software and Warranty on the Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI PredatorSense remains the prominent app on Acer’s Predator gaming laptops. On the Predator Helios Neo 16S AI, it offers power settings, system monitoring, updates, and system settings. Power profiles include quiet, balanced (the default), performance, and turbo. Performance mode indicates it overclocks the CPU and GPU, but doesn’t specify details, while turbo appears to be performance mode but with the fan speeds maxed. The app’s settings let you disable Nvidia Optimus, set up optimized battery charging, a bluelight shield, and toggle a 30-second keyboard backlighting timeout. Fan control is possible, though the custom option only allows you to set the RPM, not a curve. Most of the settings above plus lighting effects and a sound equalizer can be saved in scenario profiles. Acer loads many more apps than PredatorSense – too many: Acer Assist, Acer Chroma Tune, Acer Intelligence Space, Acer LiveArt, Acer documents, Acer Jumpstart, Acer Legal Information, Acer My Key, Acer Purified Voice Console, Acer PurifiedView, and Acer QuickPanel create a lengthy list under the Start Menu’s “A” section. Many of them are simply links to the Windows Store. Some of the apps actually installed are useful, like Acer My Key mentioned earlier. Others could be: Acer Intelligence Space provides many AI-driven features like a meeting assistant, an image generator, a media search tool, and a game assistant that claims to automatically change the color of your crosshair for maximum visibility. I didn’t test all these out – they aren’t specific to the Predator Helios Neo 16S AI – but it seems that they could add value if you’re not already vested in other AI services. There’s also a decent amount of bloatware, including a McAfee trial, a Dropbox promotion, and Forge of Empires. While easily uninstalled, they simply don’t belong on a laptop this expensive. Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI Configurations Our Predator Helios Neo 16S AI includes a Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus CPU, Nvidia RTX 5070 Ti graphics card, 16GB of dual-channel RAM, a 1TB PCIe 4.0 solid-state drive, and a 16-inch 2560 x 1600 OLED display with a 240 Hz refresh rate. It retails for $2,774.99 from Best Buy, though I did see it briefly drop to $1,999.99 during my review period. Best Buy also offers a 32GB version for $3,199.99, but it was discounted to $2,459.99 during our review period, making it less expensive than our model. Pricing is always in flux with the ongoing memory shortages, but Acer’s list prices are in line with market expectations. At Best Buy, many RTX 5070 Ti models hover around the same price as our model and many are pricier. Acer also lists a $2,099.99 model on its site with 16GB of RAM, a 1TB SSD, and an RTX 5060, though I didn’t find this model for sale. The Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI delivers on most of its thin-and-light gaming promise. Its RTX 5070 Ti provides solid gaming performance on its beautiful 240 Hz OLED display, and it follows up with a comfortable keyboard and touchpad, useful port selection, and solid upgradeability. The trouble is that its portability is undermined by its below average battery life, an ironic shortcoming for a thin-and-light laptop. Audible gaming fans and lackluster speakers are further compromises, but the limited unplugged runtime is the one that those seeking a more portable package ought to be most concerned about. But if you’re after a relatively slim gaming laptop to take between places where you can plug in, the Helios Neo 16S AI is an otherwise appealing package.

item.title: SALES: The pros and cons of using mesh Wi-Fi
item.description:
Source: Engadget
Mesh covers more ground, but a standalone router may be all you need. We may receive a commission on purchases made from links. Diving into Wi-Fi routers for the first time can be baffling. There are a lot of concepts to understand, and not just the differences between Wi-Fi 6 and 7. Speeds and features vary between models using the same specification, and it may not be clear which of your devices can (or should) connect to which frequency bands. One of the biggest purchasing decisions is whether to go with a mesh Wi-Fi system or stick to a standalone router. Most people probably default to standalone products, since they're cheaper. In fact, given the price gap, it's important to have concrete reasons for stepping up to a mesh product. The value of mesh systems mostly boils down to range and seamless roaming. In some situations, however, a standalone router may not only be acceptable, but preferable. Here's how to decide which option is right for you. The benefits and drawbacks of mesh Wi-Fi The main advantage of mesh Wi-Fi is range. In a mesh system, each satellite router acts as a sort of repeater for the gateway router that connects to your modem or fiber terminal. In theory, a relatively cheap kit like an Eero 7 two-pack can cover up to 4,000 square feet. If you need more coverage, you just add another compatible router. Conversely, standalone products have a fixed coverage radius unless you buy a Wi-Fi extender. Unlike extenders, mesh systems enable seamless transitions. There are no separate SSIDs (network IDs) — they simply hand devices off from one unit to another based on how close they are. This avoids the hassle of manual SSID selection and the problems that sometimes arise when devices need to talk to each other and assume a shared network. You also get more consistent speeds, as a signal should never degrade much unless you roam into the wider world. This seamlessness comes with downsides beyond price. Since mesh products depend on unified SSIDs, you can't assign separate IDs for each frequency band; band steering is automatic. I know from experience that mesh routers can trip up cheap 2.4GHz-only smart home accessories because their setup apps often can't find them when your phone is on 5 or 6GHz. On the flip side, you might want to force devices like PCs or VR headsets over to 5 or 6GHz for the best possible bandwidth. It's also worth noting that with cheaper mesh products, the backhaul between routers sometimes shares the same bands as connecting devices. When that happens, performance can suffer considerably. If you don't have the budget for a tri- or quad-band system, there may not be much point in going with mesh technology unless filling in dead zones is all that matters. When should you choose mesh Wi-Fi? Mesh is the obvious choice if you live in a multi-floor house, or want coverage in your backyard, detached shed or garage. A standalone router can cause smart home conflicts and create slow or dead zones, especially since metal and concrete can block signals. When interference persists, some mesh systems will even let you set up a wired Ethernet backhaul as a workaround. Most apartments should be thoroughly covered by a standalone router unless you're encountering specific speed or range issues. You're better off saving your money or putting the savings toward a faster router. There are some borderline cases. For instance, some multi-floor homes are small enough to be covered by a single router. If you want to push the limits, place your router in a relatively central location, and keep it unobscured by anything that might harm signal quality. Think of your router as a radio station — you wouldn't expect to hear the news clearly if the broadcast tower were on the opposite side of a mountain.

item.title: SALES: Your next content shoot doesn’t need a pouch of adapters
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
Have you noticed laptop prices going up lately? You’re not imagining it, and the reason has little to do with laptops. AI data centers are buying up so many memory chips that fewer are left for everyday devices. Laptop makers have raised prices or planned hikes of up to 25%, and PC shipments have dropped sharply from a year ago. If you’re a creator, that stings even more. You need a laptop that just works, but a lot of them end up costing you twice, once for the laptop and again for all the adapters you need to make it usable. You know the drill of putting the camera, lenses, batteries, and drives in the bag first. Then you toss in that little adapter pouch. If you forget it at home, your whole day slows down. Even if you remember it, there’s always that moment in a client’s office when their screen is right there, and nothing fits. So what’s the best laptop for content creators? The Dell 16S has built-in ports so that you can leave the pouch at home. It starts at $1,699.99 and is built to travel with you without sacrificing performance Two things to keep in mind when shopping PC’s right now. Some brands are holding prices steady by quietly trimming specs, so always check what a new model really offers. With memory supply expected to stay tight into 2027 or later, you will want a laptop that lasts. Because this is an investment you’ll rely on for years, you also need to trust what you see on the display. When you edit photos or video, if the colors are off, your work will look completely different on your client’s display, and nobody wants that surprise. Imagine finishing a portrait session during a sunrise shoot in the hills, sending the files off, and getting an immediate call from your client saying the skin tones look completely washed out on their monitor. That is what a true-to-life screen helps you avoid. The Dell 16S gives you a large 16-inch display with plenty of room to edit, design, and work with confidence. You can pick the version that fits how you work, and the top choice is an OLED screen if color matters to your work. Dell says it covers 100% of DCI-P3, a wide range of colors used in film, so you can spot problems before your client does. Moving from visual accuracy to sound, the dual 4W speakers with Smart Amp technology deliver surprisingly loud and clear detail when you need to check a quick clip without digging for accessories. If you are dialing in a rough cut on the drive back, you might still want to pop in your earbuds. Now, if you are stuck at an airport gate with a delayed flight, a looming deadline, and zero open wall outlets while everyone else hunts for a plug, you will still be covered. The Dell 16S delivers up to 26 hours of Netflix streaming, so you can keep working. Heavy video editing drains the battery faster than streaming, meaning you will get less time on a busy workday, but you can still leave the massive charger behind. When you sit down at your desk to wrap up final edits, you can make last-minute changes without constantly watching the battery icon drop. Performance matches that staying power. Built with modern Series 3 Intel Core Ultra processors and running smoothly on Windows 11, the system delivers fast multi-core speeds so you can export a heavy video file while sorting through raw footage simultaneously. Plus, a dedicated AI processing unit handles background tasks like generating automatic transcripts effortlessly. Walking over to meet a collaborator with the 16S is entirely stress-free. You can plug straight into a monitor or screen with the HDMI port and start your pitch without digging through a bag or breaking the flow. When you return to your setup to tackle the rest of the project, you connect your storage drive and monitor with a single cable that also charges the laptop. The two Thunderbolt 4 ports are fast, so you can copy big video files in a jiffy. You also get two regular USB ports for flash drives or a mouse, alongside a headphone jack and a small light that shows when it is charging. Best of all, you skip the extra spending on hubs and dongles, which is a real relief when everything else costs more. Opening the laptop at your desk is just as seamless, with the Full HD webcam and infrared sensors instantly recognizing your face so you can sign in without a password. PDF files are a necessary component of our multi-platform world. With this convenient file format, users are able to view and share documents across various devices, using various operating systems and software programs. While tasks such as simple viewing and/or commenting on a PDF can be accomplished with free software, there are times when you need a broader range of tools for working with a PDF document. You might want to make edits, reorganize the elements of a file, or collaborate with others to make changes. In cases such as these, you’re better served by a full-featured PDF editor. The best PDF editors allow you to edit, create, alter, and convert PDF files just like you would with any other text document. Adobe’s Acrobat Pro is full-featured PDF editor, and probably the most well known. Adobe has earned its renown honestly with an excellent feature set and overall utility. But it’s also expensive. Your PDF workloads are down by batch processing efficiently. Our picks below cover the gamut of PDF editing needs and budgets. Why you should trust PCWorld for PDF editor reviews and buying advice: At PCWorld, we’ve been testing PC hardware and software for over 40 years. Our evaluation process is always hands-on and thorough, taking into account real-world usage needs. We don’t ever recommend something we wouldn’t be comfortable using ourselves. Adobe Acrobat Pro – Best PDF editor overall - Streamlined sharing feature makes it easier to fill documents and get signatures - Rich feature set can be overwhelming for new users Adobe Acrobat Pro remains the industry standard for good reason. Its rich combination of creation, editing, reviewing, and security features are mimicked by the best alternative options, but we feel Acrobat still does it best. Its recent interface redesign makes it much easier to navigate through its robust toolset than the nested menus of yore, and its cloud subscription option puts its advanced features within reach of more individuals and small businesses. (See how it compares to the Adobe Acrobat Standard.) Though many of its features are available in other, cheaper PDF editors, Acrobat is still the editor against which all others are judged. Not surprisingly, Acrobat Pro includes an Al assistant, albeit not at an additional $4.99 per month. Depending on your PDF editing needs, the AI’s ability to summarize, answer questions, or extract key details from documents could earn its keep in valuable time saved. See our article on “5 ways Adobe Acrobat’s AI Assistant gives you a productivity edge.” - Intuitive Microsoft Office ribbon-style interface A fully featured PDF editor that can go toe-to-toe with Acrobat Pro’s feature set, Nitro PDF is a less costly alternative by about $60 per year. Its full suite of PDF editing features cover the range of needs and scenarios: content editing; review and markup; form fill and signing; and multiple security options for sensitive documents including permissions, password protection, and data redaction. It even facilitates adding, removing, and editing bates numbering in legal documents. A Microsoft Office-style ribbon interface makes workflows feel familiar and intuitive. The addition of AI is judicious, and can provide practical assistance such as by summarizing PDFs and allowing you to ask questions about content. But don’t just take our word for Nitro PDF’s impressive capabilities. You can learn that first hand by taking advantage of Nitro PDF’s 14-day free trial. No credit card is required and none of the features are locked — there’s nothing like a test drive to persuade you. EaseUS PDF Editor – Best cheap PDF editor - Annotation options enable easy collaboration - Needs subscription to remove usage limits EaseUS PDF Editor might not have the name recognition of some of the other editors on this list, but it’s more than capable of holding its own in the crowded PDF editor market. It provides all of the essential tools for managing PDF files without any of the elaborate or hard-to-understand features. It allows users to jump right in to their toolset and get straight to editing. While EaseUS’s features are great, they are also pretty standard fare among PDF editors. What makes it stand out among the pack is its affordable price—$29.95 a month, $49.95 annually, or $79.95 for a lifetime license. It’s a great value for those who regularly edit PDFs and don’t want to pay out the nose. EaseUS also offers a fully functional free version (with embedded watermarks on your edited documents) so users can take it for a spin to see if it meets their needs before they commit to paying any money. PDF Candy is the rare free PDF editor that offers a lot of the features you’d typically have to pay for. We’re talking scanning, multiple file-conversion options, and OCR functionality. A whopping 98 tools in all. This is what makes PDF Candy stand out among the multitude of lesser free PDF editors. Of course, being free, there are compromises. In this case, the interface is a little disjointed, with the tool icons lacking any discernible organizing principle. But once you get familiar with the layout, you’re off and running. There’s also the fact of being limited to one PDF task per hour with the free version. This is a non-issue if your needs are modest and consist of the occasional PDF editing task. If you want unfettered access, you need to shell out $6 per month, or $48 per year. - Comprehensive editing and annotation tools - Lifetime license enables use on Mac only PDF Expert is an excellent editor that fits seamlessly into the Apple ecosystem, making it our pick for Macs, iPads, and iPhone users. While macOS does include a PDF editor in its Preview app, iOS devices don’t have a native PDF editor and PDF Expert fills that gap nicely. It has a clean and intuitive interface and offers a plethora of easy-to-use editing options such as page management, converting scanned files into editable documents, and conversion to other file formats, among other things. The pricing plan is also considerably cheaper than most of the other top picks, meaning this is a no-brainer for Apple users. In its latest iteration, PDF Expert includes and AI-powered chat assistant that can be particularly helpful with long or complex documents. For example, it can extract key points, summarize information, and generate hashtags as a navigation aid. Apple Preview PDF editor – Best free PDF editor for Mac - PDFs can be protected with passwords, encryption, and permission controls Mac users needn’t look beyond the macOS for their PDF editing needs, since there is a full set of PDF markup tools already available at their disposal in Apple Preview. It has the chops to handle most personal and business PDF editing needs, including encryption, password protection, and permissions for files. Apple Preview’s PDF features and capabilities are impressive and should be all you need for most common editing tasks. The drawback, of course, is that only Mac users can take advantage of them. - Business features won’t be needed by some users - Requires annual commitment to get best value pdfFiller is a browser-based PDF editor that allows you do to just about everything PDF-related—editing, securing, sharing, creating, and storing PDF files—all from its intuitive and simple web interface. Its design is similar to a desktop app, with the toolbar across the top, and document thumbnails along the side, so it’s very easy to select the page you want to work on and perform the desired function, be it adding, deleting, or copying/pasting text; changing font style, size, and color; and so on. A standard set of markup tools is also available. It has a surprisingly deep set of features for both personal and business use. For instance the Premium plan offers an impressive legal document library, as well as SignNow support. While incredibly versatile, not all of pdfFiller’s advanced features will suit everyone. Fortunately, there are three subscription tiers, which gives users a way to meet their editing needs without paying extra for unnecessary features: Basic for $8/mo; Plus for $12/mo; Premium for $15/mo with an annual commitment. Month-to-month options are also available, but at a higher cost, of course. - MyPDFTools: This handy, free PDF toolkit offers easy and effective basics, but more demanding jobs expose some limitations. - Swifdoo PDF for Windows: This full-featured, low-priced Acrobat alternative should serve most users well, with most everything you’d need for editing PDFs. - MobiPDF: Budget buyers will find a lot to like about PDF Extra. It offers good basic-to-intermediate PDF functionality that will please both casual and professional users, for a fraction of the cost of pinnacle program Adobe Acrobat Pro. - PDF24 Creator: This is a capable free editor that comes in handy for casual use, but if you need a program for more regular editing duties, PDF24 Creator has annoyances that will hinder its helpfulness. - PDF-XChange Editor: Another full-featured PDF editor that will fulfill most editing needs for a reasonable price. It also offers a respectable free version, if you can accept its watermarks. - Kofax Power PDF 5: This is a close alternative to Adobe Acrobat Pro with essential and advanced editing tools and lots of help resources, making it suitable for old hands and those new to PDF editing. Who curated this article? Michael Ansaldo is PCWorld’s primary PDF reviewer. He’s a veteran tech journalist who has been reviewing and writing about hardware, software, and services for a variety of publications including TechHive, Wired, Macworld, Mac|Life, Mobile Magazine, Enterprise.Nxt, Executive Travel, and others. He was formerly PCWorld’s Small Business Editor. Why spend a chunk of change on a desktop editor when free online PDF editors abound? The simple answer is because you get what you pay for. Generally, free online editors will let you add text and comments, merge and split documents, and convert files to and from PDF. With rare exception, however, they won’t let you edit existing text and many have file-size and page-volume restrictions. And a lot of them will watermark your edited document. For these reasons, web PDF editors are best reserved for simple, fast editing jobs. Call in these big dogs for anything more demanding. PDF editors come in a variety of flavors, offering varying feature sets—from basic functionality to power-user tools. It’s important to know what features best match your workflow before you commit to a PDF editor. The most fundamental function of a PDF editor is to make PDFs, either from scratch, scanned hard copies, or by converting digital documents. A good PDF editor should be able to transform a variety of file types—from Microsoft Office formats to images to HTML—and do so seamlessly, preserving the original formatting. It should also include OCR technology to make the PDF text searchable and editable. Likewise, a good PDF editor must be able to export PDFs into other editable formats such as Microsoft Word and PowerPoint, HTML, or plain text, maintaining the original files hyperlinks, images, and other elements. Another bit of magic that PDF editors unlock is the ability to modify text; insert, resize, and move images; and reorganize pages in the PDF. A good one will perform these tasks as easily as in a text document or slide deck, allowing in-line editing, dragging-and dropping graphics, and adding or removing hyperlinks. A good PDF editor should also let you or anyone else using it add comments and other annotations to PDF files during review. It should have tools to mark up both text documents and graphic-heavy files like webpages. Common options include sticky notes, callout boxes, highlighting, freehand drawing tools, and stamps with messages like “approved,” “revised,” and “confidential.” All businesses deal with documents containing sensitive data. Look for a PDF editor that includes security features that allow access for authorized eyes only. Good options will usually offer several levels of security, including password protection, permissions setting, and content redaction, which “blacks out” selected text and images. Most PDF editors will also offer one or more ways to electronically sign documents. While deep PDF editing is best done on a desktop, it’s nice to be able to review and annotate files when you’re out and about. While PDFs can typically be reviewed in any PDF reader or editor, regardless of which one they were created in, consider looking for an editor that has a dedicated mobile app, is optimized for mobile devices, or allows cloud access to features through a mobile browser. One of the great things about a PDF is that it can be read and edited in any PDF program regardless of which one it was created in. So beyond the features outlined here, let your personal preferences guide you in making your decision. What is the best PDF editor? If you want a PDF editor that truly does it all, PCWorld’s pick is Adobe Acrobat Pro. It’s the industry standard for a reason. As a subscription-based product, you can count on it to always be up to date, in terms of patches and feature enhancements. That also grants you access to a mobile version that’s both robust and user friendly. What is the difference between a PDF document and a PDF form? While there are a number of different types of PDF file formats, they all fall under the umbrella term of PDF documents. A PDF form is a type of PDF document that has editable form fields a user can fill out. Typically, parts of the document are static and can’t be changed in a PDF form, such as questions in a survey or instructions about filling out the form. In a PDF form, the content fields a user fills out are open to editing and can offer a list of possible answer options or can be written in freely. Are PDF documents and Word files different? Yes. They are two entirely different document formats. While you can export from one file format to another, they are not the same. Word file formats are usually used for word processing, editing, and making changes to text. PDF documents on the other hand, are most often utilized for viewing, sharing, and printing. Additionally, Word files are read and write and contain some version of the “.doc” file format. Whereas PDF files are typically read-only and contain the “.pdf” file format. Can you protect PDF documents from being edited by other people? Yes. If you have a PDF document that you don’t want anyone else to edit, you can protect the file. You can do this by opening the file in Acrobat, for instance, and clicking Tools > Protect. Then you have a few options as to whether you want to simply restrict editing with a password, or if you want to encrypt the file for further safety. Once you choose how you want to protect the PDF document, you can set a password and save. Can you merge PDFs with a free PDF editor? As a matter of fact, many free PDF editors allow you to merge two or more PDFs into one document. Such is the case with our top free pick PDF Candy. Open up the PDF editor application or website in your browser and search for the Merge option. It will then ask you to add the files of all PDFs you wish to merge. Once the files have been added, arrange the page order and alignment before proceeding with the merge. Afterwards, all of your previously PDF files will be merged into one new PDF document. Does Google have a free PDF editor? Yes and no. Google doesn’t provide a designated free PDF editor itself, but there are third-party Chrome extensions that you can use to help get the job done. Alternatively, you can make use of Google Drive to edit a PDF document. Simply upload the document onto your Google Drive and then select the file and right-click and select Open with > Google Docs. The file will be opened as an editable Google Docs text document. Then just make your edits and when you’re finished click File > Download >PDF Document to revert it back to a PDF file. This method is a quick and easy way to edit a simple PDF document, but be careful as Google Docs can run into formatting issues if your original document has complex visual formatting such as tables and graphs. In this case, it is best to use a designated free or premium PDF editor.

item.title: SALES: 7 of my favorite free (and fully optimized) iPhone Duo apps so far — from PianoFold to Spotify
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
If you’ve been weighing up whether to spend a small fortune on the iPhone Duo, you’re probably already aware of the software-related criticism surrounding it. At the time of writing, several high-profile non-Apple apps (including LinkedIn, Google Calendar, and Duolingo) still haven’t been optimized to take advantage of the Duo’s dual-screen form factor (read: they look awful). But less has been written about the apps and games that have received a Duo-specific facelift. I’ve been using the Duo for a few weeks now, and in this guide, I’ve highlighted seven fully optimized (and free) apps whose slick performance bodes well for the future of Apple’s first foldable. PianoFold is, hands down, my favorite iPhone Duo game so far. It’s basically Guitar Hero, but for the piano — musical tiles glide down from the top of the screen, and you have to tap the appropriate tile as it reaches the bottom of the screen to play the correct melody. PianoFold works in every iPhone Duo orientation. If you fold it like a laptop, the notes fall from the upright half and strike just below the hinge. If you hold it open flat, the notes strike halfway down the screen. And if you use the Duo closed, the game functions as it would on any single-screen iPhone. I prefer to play in the unfolded landscape mode, but the half-folded mode looks exceptionally cool if you enable ‘Room view’, which uses the Duo’s camera to make the notes appear as if they’re floating through your surroundings. The full version of PianoFold costs money, but the free version is great in its own right. You get access to seven classical songs — including “Ode to Joy” (easy), “The Entertainer” (hard), and “Can-Can” (impossible) — but once you clear the first five, one song from the full game is made free each day until midnight. Battlefleet Duo reinvents the classic two-player strategy game, Battleship, for the 21st-century iPhone Duo-owning consumer. Tabletop mode lets your Duo double as the traditional Battleship box — your fleet is displayed on one side, and your enemy’s (hidden) fleet is displayed on the other — while unfolded mode fills the screen with enhanced 3D graphics; fires rage, ships sink, and the weather changes on a dime. There’s even a Classic mode, which switches out these modern frills for the game’s original plastic board, ships, and pegs. As with PianoFold, Battlefleet Duo is only partially free, but the unpaid version gives you two free games per day against the AI, a friend, or online players. And if you have the patience to play more than two games of Battleship per day, more power to you. Art of Flora is as simple as iPhone games come: you piece together puzzles depicting botanical illustrations, and you’re rewarded with a description of the plant in question. This slower-paced game is designed to relax and educate, and the iPhone Duo-specific version supports big-screen puzzle-completing in both landscape and portrait orientations. The first 10 puzzles in Art of Flora are free — the other 100 can be purchased via packs and bundles — but in my experience, that’s enough to see you through a train journey or kill some time on a flight. Once you’ve completed the lot, jump straight into the Duo’s Books app to make yourself feel like a regular Charles Darwin. Pools is described by its developer as “slow, reflective, and intentionally uneventful,” but don’t download this game thinking it’s going to relax you. This Duo-optimized title is a psychological horror walking simulator inspired by The Backrooms internet lore and, specifically, Jared Pike’s "Dream Pools" 3D renderings. Pools has no puzzles, no user interface (UI), and no enemies — you’re just dropped into its liminal spaces and left to explore at your own pace/risk (delete as appropriate). This game is also my favorite showcase for the power of Apple’s A20 Pro chipset. It looks absolutely gorgeous in all graphics presets (Quality, Performance, or Ultra), offering genuinely console-quality light and water physics. You’ll get similar performance from Pools on the iPhone 18 Pro, but the Duo’s larger inner screen makes it both easier to play and more enjoyable to gawk at. Lo and behold, the free version of Pools features just one chapter (or map) — the other six require a one-time purchase — but it’s big enough to show what Apple’s first foldable is made of. I don’t need to tell you what Spotify is, but if you’re an existing Spotify user who’s worried about the experience of using Spotify on the iPhone Duo, don’t be: it’s awesome. Well, it’s awesome when using the Duo unfolded. When closed, you still get that jarring black bar on the right-hand side of the screen, but in unfolded mode, Spotify splits the screen in half to show your playlist on one side and your currently playing song on the other. This split-screen works in both landscape and portrait orientations, and while Spotify still needs to make better use of Apple’s vertical nav bar even in unfolded mode, I’ve been enjoying my time with the world’s most popular music streaming app on the iPhone Duo. Here’s one for the workers: Slack on the iPhone Duo works like a dream. This is one of the few third-party apps (at the time of writing) that uses the Duo’s larger inner canvas and Apple’s vertical nav bar, so you can access channels, direct message chats, and menu options in a single view. Slack on the iPhone Duo basically puts the Slack desktop experience in the palm(s) of your hand, and while it’s obviously less usable in folded form, it’s still been optimized for the Duo’s outer screen in a way that 90% of apps just aren’t right now. Working 24/7 has never looked so good! If you’re reading this from the US, Australia, or anywhere in the UK that isn’t London, I’m sorry to disappoint or bore you, but the official TfL (Transport for London) app is a sight to behold on the iPhone Duo. This is one of the last apps I expected to be optimized for Apple’s first folding phone, but to my surprise, it was one of the first. There’s no split-screen functionality, but the London Underground map looks glorious when plastered across all 7.6 inches of the Duo’s nano-texture display, and it’s great fun to traverse the 272-station network while, erm, stuck on the London Underground. So there you have it: seven of the best free, fully optimized iPhone Duo apps I've come across so far. Of course, plenty more apps have been optimized for Apple’s first foldable than those I've mentioned here (my colleague, Lance, has highlighted one of his favorites on TikTok, as have we on YouTube), and plenty more will become optimized in the coming weeks as developers roll out Duo-specific updates. item.title: SALES: 10 Best Winter Hiking Boots
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com
Today’s winter hiking boots are waterproof, insulated, and compatible with traction aids such as microspikes and snowshoes. While 200-gram insulated mids are fine for commuting and half-day hikes down to about 10-20 degrees (F), we recommend buying boots with higher calf coverage and 400-gram insulation for all-day hikes and mountain climbs in colder temperatures. We are experienced winter hikers with hundreds of successful mountain summits, and we understand what it takes to stay safe and comfortable on long, challenging winter hikes. Here are our top 10 winter hiking boot recommendations: 1. Oboz Bridger 10″ Insulated Winter Boots 2. KEEN Revel IV High Polar Winter Boots 5. Oboz Bridger 8″ Insulated Winter Mids 10. Columbia Bugaboot III Insulated Winter Boots You can’t use your regular 3-season boots or shoes for winter hiking because they lack waterproofing and insulation. Most insulated winter hiking boots are guaranteed waterproof out of the box. Many have rubber or waterproof synthetic soles, so you don’t have to worry about water soaking into the fabric. If moisture does get into your boots, insulated winter boots will still keep your feet warm. The same isn’t true of leather hiking boots, even when treated with waterproofing creams and sprays. If your regular hiking boots absorb water in winter, they can freeze and cause frostbite. Winter boots should be waterproof and insulated to keep your feet dry and warm, have laces for a secure fit, be comfortable enough to wear all day, and be compatible with traction aids like microspikes and snowshoes. While the insulation you need varies, winter boots with non-removable synthetic insulation are the lightest and therefore the easiest to hike in. Synthetic boots are also lighter and more waterproof than leather boots. Some boot manufacturers provide temperature ratings, but there’s no standard way to measure how warm winter boots are. Understand that these ratings are estimates at best and that users will have varying experiences based on their activity level, health, weight, sex, metabolism, and other factors. Most 400 g insulated winter hiking boots suit all-day winter hikes and snowshoeing in subzero temperatures. They have calf-high uppers, which makes them warmer than mids because more of your lower leg is covered by insulation. Many manufacturers claim they’ll keep your feet warm down to -40F, but that assumes you’re actively hiking, not sitting around doing nothing. Realistically, they work best in temperatures from 30F down to -15F. If you plan to climb 4000-footers in winter in New Hampshire’s White Mountains, the Adirondacks, Maine, or Vermont, we recommend using 400 g boots. Most 200 g winter hiking boots are ankle-high mids and retain less heat on the lower leg than calf-height 400g boots. On the other hand, they’re a little easier to hike in because they’re lighter and feel more like regular hiking boots. 200 g boots suit temperatures from 30°F to 10°F and are ideal for milder winter conditions and shorter hikes, where you’re less likely to get caught out after dark when temperatures drop. Mountaineering boots have rigid soles that work with crampons that lack flexible center bars, for rugged mountains with steeper slopes or thick ice. You can hike in them, but it feels very different from a soft-soled 400g or 200g insulated winter hiking boot. Most insulated mountaineering boot manufacturers don’t rate their boots’ temperature ranges, so you have to rely on anecdotal word-of-mouth about how warm they are. If you hike across glaciers or go on trips led by mountaineering guides, it’s usually best to ask them which boots to bring. They may even rent you boots. While you should take the manufacturer’s temperature ratings with a grain of salt, they are a good indicator of a boot’s relative warmth. It’s difficult to compare warmth between boots with different insulation, but knowing how much insulation a boot has can help you compare models from the same manufacturer. This is like a regular boot tongue, except the sides are closed and sewn to the boot sides to prevent water from leaking in when you step in puddles. In addition to providing more protection, a beefy toe cap won’t collapse when you wear microspikes or crampons. Your boots’ soles should provide good traction on loose or packed snow. Look for boots with a deep tread, like a Vibram sole, though you’ll likely augment your boot with microspikes. Look for boots with a soft cuff that closes off the gap between your leg and boot. A gaiter ring is a small ring attached to the top of the boot that you can hook your gaiters onto. It’s not the end of the world if your boots don’t have one since you can still hook the gaiter to your boot laces.

item.title: SALES: Apple’s $50 Intelligence Usage Packs extend access to some AI features
item.description:
Source: The Verge
After publishing a support article in early September outlining usage limits for some Apple Intelligence features, the company has updated Logic Pro with an option to “Buy More Usage” for a one-time purchase price of $49.99, as spotted by 9to5Mac. It has a built-in AI assistant to do things like “start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project.” Apple’s $50 Intelligence Usage Packs extend access to some AI features Logic Pro is Apple’s first app to charge for extended usage of Apple Intelligence. These Intelligence Usage Packs, as Apple calls them, will allow users to continue accessing certain Apple Intelligence features that have usage limits because they rely on cloud-based AI models from OpenAI or Google Gemini. The Usage Packs can only be used by the Apple Account that purchased them (Family Sharing isn’t supported) and, as Apple explains on its website, any unused additional usage will roll over from month to month, but will expire 12 months after it was purchased. For Logic Pro, Apple says the usage limit is “impacted by the complexity of conversations you have with the assistant.” Users finding themselves running out of access can find the option to buy an Intelligence Usage Pack in the Intelligence Features > Show Usage section of the app’s main menu. Currently, only Logic Pro has the option to buy more usage, but it’s expected to be added to other Apple Creator Studio apps this month, including Pixelmator Pro, Final Cut Pro, Motion, plus Pages, Keynote, and Numbers that are getting access to Apple’s AI chatbot.
